query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: High-throughput computational thermodynamic modeling combined with machine learning can accurately and efficiently determine the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties of high-entropy alloys within a well-characterized compositional range.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys with diverse compositions and near-random multi-principal element distributions.
generation.intervention: High-throughput computational thermodynamic modeling combined with machine learning algorithms
generation.conditions: The approach is applied to HEAs under controlled heating conditions and within a compositional space that has been previously characterized by experimental and simulation data.
generation.structural_mediator: Underlying atomic-scale interactions and local chemical environments that govern thermodynamic behaviors across the solid-liquid transition.
generation.mechanism: The method uses computational models to capture fundamental physical interactions and free-energy landscapes, while machine learning leverages existing data to interpolate and extrapolate thermodynamic properties efficiently.
generation.predicted_outcome: Predicted melting temperatures, fusion enthalpies and entropies, volume changes at melting, and liquid-phase properties will quantify within approximately 5–10% of experimental measurements.
generation.baseline: Traditional experimental techniques and standalone computational methods that are typically more time-consuming or less precise for exploring large compositional spaces.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to perform reliably only for high-entropy alloys whose compositions are within the calibrated range and that maintain single-phase stability under the test conditions.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the method's accuracy for alloys outside the validated compositional space or those with significant phase segregation or non-equilibrium effects at high temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize and characterize a diverse set of high-entropy alloys that were not used during model training. For each alloy, use the computational and machine learning approach to predict the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase properties. Compare these predictions with high-precision experimental measurements obtained via techniques such as differential scanning calorimetry, dilatometry, and in situ x-ray diffraction.
measurements: Melting temperature from DSC or dilatometry
Enthalpy and entropy of fusion from integrated DSC signals
Volume change at melting from dilatometry
Liquid-phase thermodynamic properties from in situ diffraction
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted values deviate from the experimental measurements by more than approximately 10% for the majority of the tested alloys (more than 20%), the proposed approach will be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Integrating CALPHAD modeling with machine learning trained on first‐principles molecular dynamics data will enable the accurate and efficient prediction of the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties for high-entropy alloys.
drafts.material_initial_state: Solid high-entropy alloys exhibiting near-random multi-principal element distributions.
drafts.intervention: Application of a hybrid modeling approach that combines traditional CALPHAD assessments with machine learning surrogates built on ab initio molecular dynamics simulation data.
drafts.conditions: Equilibrium heating under controlled low-pressure conditions; compositions falling within the range where atomic sizes, mixing enthalpies, and configurational entropies do not cause extreme segregation or ordering effects.
drafts.structural_mediator: The short-range atomic ordering and local chemical environments within the alloy that influence the free energy landscape across the solid-liquid transition.
drafts.mechanism: The approach leverages first-principles molecular dynamics to generate accurate energetic and volumetric data near melting. This data is then used to recalibrate and refine CALPHAD free-energy models via machine learning, thereby capturing complex compositional effects inherent in high-entropy systems. The combined model is expected to better resolve the thermodynamic driving forces of melting transitions across a broad compositional spectrum.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Predictions of melting temperature will be within approximately ±50 K and fusion enthalpy within roughly ±10% of experimental values, outperforming conventional CALPHAD methods which generally have larger uncertainties (e.g., ±100 K or more in T_m). Liquid-phase structural properties and volume changes are expected to be similarly defined by reduced relative errors.
drafts.baseline: Traditional CALPHAD techniques or experimental-only approaches that either suffer from broad uncertainties or require bulky experimental campaigns.
drafts.boundary: The method is expected to work well for high-entropy alloys with similar atomic sizes and moderate mixing enthalpies. It may not be applicable to alloys where pronounced elemental segregation, drastic size mismatch, or non-equilibrium phase formation dominate the melting behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a diverse set of high-entropy alloys covering the expected compositional space. For each alloy, predict the melting properties using the proposed hybrid approach. Independently determine the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and liquid-phase volume change using high-precision differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), high-energy x-ray diffraction, and dilatometry during controlled heating experiments.
measurements: Enthalpy and entropy of fusion from integrated DSC signals
Volume change at melting from dilatometry
Liquid-phase structural properties from in situ x-ray diffraction
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted melting temperature deviates from experimental values by more than ±100 K, or if the predicted fusion enthalpy/entropy errors exceed ±20%, or if liquid-phase structural indicators do not match within acceptable experimental uncertainty, then the hybrid modeling approach is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A combined CALPHAD–DFT–machine-learning approach can accurately and efficiently predict the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change upon melting, and other liquid-phase thermodynamic properties (with <5–10% average error) across single-phase high-entropy alloys by leveraging high-throughput theoretical calculations and sparse experimental data for model validation.
drafts.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys that are near or at single-phase stability prior to melting (e.g., equiatomic or nearly equiatomic compositions).
drafts.intervention: Integrate ab initio (DFT) computed energies and vibrational properties into thermodynamic databases (CALPHAD) and train machine-learning models on available experimental thermodynamic data for meso- and high-dimensional composition spaces.
drafts.conditions: Homogeneous solid-solution HEAs maintained under controlled heating to their respective melting ranges, ensuring minimal phase decomposition or precipitation.
drafts.structural_mediator: Electron-density and partial bonding descriptors derived from DFT, providing fundamental energy and vibrational inputs for machine-learning featurization and refining CALPHAD parameters.
drafts.mechanism: The synergy between first-principles calculations and data-driven modeling captures chemical complexity and local atomic interactions, enabling robust extrapolation of high-temperature thermodynamic behaviors.
drafts.predicted_outcome: For new multi-principal-element compositions that remain single-phase at high temperatures, the predicted melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change, and other liquid-phase thermochemical properties will deviate by less than approximately 5–10% from measured values.
drafts.baseline: Experimental thermophysical property measurements for known single-phase alloys, plus existing CALPHAD descriptions of simpler systems for model calibration.
drafts.boundary: Applicable primarily to single-phase high-entropy alloys with minimal ordering or chemical segregation at relevant temperatures; extended validation would be needed for complex multi-phase or metastable alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize and characterize multiple new high-entropy alloy compositions with diverse principal element ratios that were not included in the model training set, then measure their high-temperature thermodynamic properties via differential scanning calorimetry (for enthalpy and entropy of fusion) and laser melting (for melting temperature and volume changes).
measurements: 1) Melting temperature using onset of melting in DSC or dilatometry.
2) Enthalpy and entropy of fusion from integrated DSC signals.
3) Density measurement before and after melting to assess volume change.
4) Phase stability and compositional homogeneity with in situ diffraction or microscopy.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the machine-learning–based predictions systematically deviate from experimental measurements by more than ~10% for these newly tested compositions, the hypothesis is falsified.
